evidence.locator: P052:p0004:s0002; exact span beginning 'Once a planning problem is formulated'
evidence.source_content:
Once a planning problem is formulated as the constrained optimization problem, it can be rigor-
ously solved by solvers such as the SMT solver. Therefore, we propose an pipeline that solves the
planning problem by converting them into constrained optimization problems and then solving them
using the SMT solver. Our pipeline consists of the following steps, as shown in Fig. 1. ❶DEFINER:
LLMFP first prompts an LLM to define the constrained optimization problem from the user inputs,
P = D(d, i) (Sec. 3.2). ❷FORMULATOR: LLMFP asks LLM to think about the necessary vari-
ables and steps to build when programming, and formulate a representation to summarize all key
information of these variables (Sec. 3.3). ❸CODE GENERATOR: Given this representation, LLMs
generate codes that initialize all necessary variables, assert constraints, and add goals (Sec. 3.4).
evidence.codex_note: P052 decomposes formalization into problem definition, variable representation, and solver-code generation.

vert the execution result into a fixed format and provide a short assessment of the execution results
(Sec. 3.5). ❺SELF ASSESSMENT AND MODIFICATION: LLMFP assesses each step based on
the execution result, and modifies the first incorrect step (Sec. 3.6). The generated plan is delivered
when it passes self-assessments of all steps. Please refer to Appendix A.9 and A.10 for example
outputs and prompts of all steps in LLMFP.

evidence.locator: P053:p0004:s0001; exact extracted span beginning 'We call a planning problem an unraveling prob-'
evidence.source_content:
We call a planning problem an unraveling prob-
lem when the natural language description Dn is
succinct, but the denoted planning instance
U(Dn) = In = ⟨On, Fn, An, In, Gn⟩
is significantly larger (|Dn| ≪|In|). This creates
a distinct scaling challenge for a Formalizer that
must still explicitly emit polynomially many facts
from the compact description.
To address this compression gap, we intro-
duce the paradigm of LLM-as-Higher-Order-
Formalizer. Instead of directly outputting the fully
grounded instance In, the model outputs a higher-
order generator program first:
Dn 7→Rn 7→In,
where Rn compactly describes (e.g., in Python)
how to emit the objects and fluents of the instance.
A downstream compiler, interpreter, or lifted plan-
ner then expands this higher-order representation
into a grounded planning instance. While a regu-
lar Formalizer navigates the ground fluent space
Fn, an H-O Formalizer instead navigates a com-
pact program space; its generated text can remain
small even when the denoted instance is large
(|Rn| ≪|Fn|). This shifts Formalizer’s burden
from enumerating large grounded fluent sets to pro-
ducing a compact generation rule of them.
evidence.codex_note: P053 moves the model from enumerating grounded fluents to emitting a compact generator program.

needed to write code for repeating patterns such
as object types appending and loops to formalize
the problems, we use two-stage prompts where we
ask the LLMs to reflect on the repeating patterns

nalizing the Python programs, especially paying
attention to possible errors in the way problem
descriptions translate to repeating patterns. This

evidence.locator: P054:p0007:s0001; exact extracted span beginning 'This suggests that a more natural-sounding'
evidence.source_content:
This suggests
that a more natural-sounding domain and prob-
lem description is much more challenging than
templated, less natural sounding descriptions. One
potential explanation is that pattern matching a tem-
plate back to PDDL is much easier than having to
first parse all the predicates and objects from a pas-
sage. Another reason is a more natural sounding
description may leave out implicit common-sense.
For example, the Natural BlocksWorld-100 data

because any human who reads that a block is “on

on top of it and hence ‘clear’ to be moved. How-

and will leave out the ‘clear’ predicate, leading to
unsolvable PDDL or incorrect plans.

evidence.locator: P076:p0005:s0001; exact extracted span beginning 'To operationalize the MAS hijacking attack (defi'
evidence.source_content:
To operationalize the MAS hijacking attack (defined formally in Appendix C), our attacker
crafts a false (but plausible) error message. This message is formatted similarly to genuine
error notifications (e.g., in Python or WordPress) but, instead of legitimate remediation
steps, it contains malicious instructions for individual agents. In particular, the attacker
targets inter-agent communication by specifying how each agent should act in the ensuing
“conversation.” For examples of malicious error messages, see Appendix H. Depending on
their access (Section 3), the attacker then disseminates this content via a local file, webpage,
or another medium. The attack exploits inter-agent trust and leverages adaptive error-
handling behavior intended to enhance the MAS’s benign functionality.

We believe this attack is successful because it “launders” adversarial requests through
outputs and metadata of front-line agents that directly interact with untrusted content. This
is critical for two reasons. First, it enables the request to reach the orchestrator. In MAS
configurations we tested, orchestrators do not directly interact with untrusted content (file-
access and Web agents do, but they do not execute code directly). Therefore, the adversary
cannot perform indirect prompt injection (IPI) directly on the orchestrator. Second, laun-
dering the request through another agent’s metadata significantly changes its presentation
(formatting, phrasing, etc.). We conjecture that safety alignment of the underlying LLMs
involved training them on conventional IPI strings but not on presentations created as a
result of our attack (the LLMs in our experiments are black-box and the details of their
training are not available). In this sense, the attack is creating a previously unknown type of
jailbreaking templates. We test these conjectures in Subsection 6.4.
evidence.codex_note: Untrusted content is laundered through front-line Agent metadata into orchestrator control decisions.

evidence.locator: P076:p0008:s0001; exact extracted span beginning 'Execution of recognized harmful code. In one Cre'
evidence.source_content:
Execution of recognized harmful code. In one CrewAI experiment, after reasoning that
executing the reverse shell code may be unsafe, the orchestrator resolved to proceed safely.
To hone its safe file-reading process, it created a dummy file to read and read it, only to
“realize” that the dummy file was not what the user wanted. The orchestrator then re-read
the attack file using its newly minted process and executed the reverse shell as commanded
(see Appendix J). Similarly, in another AutoGen experiment, after the coder agent refused to
produce malicious code, the file surfer sub-agent produced its own reverse shell, helpfully
noting to not execute the code because it was dangerous. The generated code was then
executed by the code executor, opening a reverse shell (see Appendix K). In several other
CrewAI experiments, the coding agent recognized that the reverse shell code was malicious
and generated inline warnings. Nevertheless, it failed to relay this information to the rest
of the system. Instead, it signaled success to the orchestrator, which then commanded the
coder to execute the code, ultimately resulting in a breach.
evidence.codex_note: Individual Agent warnings or refusals can coexist with system-level execution by another Agent.

evidence.source_content:
As shown in Fig.2(a), NQ reaches
near-optimal performance with a single search step,
while additional steps provide little benefit. In con-
trast, Bamboogle requires up to three steps to peak,
after which further searches reduce performance.
Fig. 2(b) further shows that exceeding the near-
optimal depth leads to a notable increase in the over-
searching ratio for both datasets, with the effect
being more pronounced on the more complex Ban-
boogle dataset. These results indicate that the ap-
propriate search depth is task-dependent, with a
minimal sufficient depth achieves near-optimal
accuracy while mitigating over-searching.
3.2
What Affects Appropriate Search Depth?
Different LLMs exhibit varying reasoning and re-
trieval capabilities, which in turn affect their answer
accuracy in agentic RAG systems. This raises a
natural question: does the agent’s capability also
influence the appropriate search depth? To inves-
tigate this, we conduct controlled experiments on
the Bamboogle dataset using Qwen-3B, Qwen-7B,
and Qwen-14B models, each performing a range
of search steps to answer the same set of questions.
As shown in Fig. 2(c), the 3B model steadily im-
proves with increasing search depth, achieving its
peak performance at the final search step within
the evaluated range. In contrast, the 7B and 14B
models reach their optimal performance at the sec-
ond and third search steps, respectively, after which
additional searches lead to performance degrada-
tion. Fig. 2(d) further shows that over-searching
becomes increasingly pronounced as search depth
grows, with stronger models exhibiting more pro-
nounced degradation. Taken together, these results
from the previous and current subsections indicate
that the minimal sufficient search depth, which
balances accuracy and efficiency, is jointly deter-
mined by question complexity and the agent’s
capability.

chain (i.e., using the output of one tool as an input
for another tool). This is due to the fact that API
calls for each tool are generated independently; as a
consequence, there are no examples of chained tool
use in the ﬁnetuning dataset. Our current approach
also does not allow the LM to use a tool in an in-

engines, that could potentially return hundreds of
different results, enabling a LM to browse through
these results or to reﬁne its search query in a simi-

certain applications. Beyond this, we found models
trained with Toolformer to often be sensitive to the
exact wording of their input when deciding whether
or not to call an API; this is perhaps unsurprising
given that LMs are known to be very sensitive to
the prompt they are provided with in both zero-
and few-shot settings (Jiang et al., 2020; Schick
and Schütze, 2021a). Depending on the tool, our
method is also very sample-inefﬁcient; for example,
processing more than a million documents results
in only a few thousand examples of useful calls
to the calculator API. A potential solution to this
problem might be to iteratively apply our approach,
similar to how this is done in related bootstrapping
approaches (Schick and Schütze, 2021a; Izacard
and Grave, 2021; Parisi et al., 2022). Finally, when
deciding whether or not to make an API call, Tool-
former currently does not take into account the
tool-dependent, computational cost incurred from
making an API call.

on average and exhibiting limited consistency
across models. Monitoring-based defenses proved

the monitoring LLM often oscillating between

clear or consistent pattern across different domains
or attack types. Additional details and discussion
can be found in Appendix D.4.

Over-

deployment-oriented defenses provide only lim-
ited robustness against adversarial attacks. While
techniques such as paraphrasing and output de-
limitation can reduce attack success rates in cer-
tain cases, their improvements are modest and of-
ten inconsistent across models and attack types.
Monitoring-based defenses further suffer from in-
stability, frequently producing false positives and
failing to reliably distinguish between benign and
adversarial behaviors. In contrast, more sophisti-
cated defense strategies such as robust agent align-
ment, or architecture-level safeguards have the po-
tential to offer stronger and more consistent de-
fenses. However, these approaches typically come
with significant trade-offs: they may require sub-
stantial system redesign, additional training data
and compute, or tighter integration between compo-
nents, thereby increasing deployment complexity
and runtime overhead.

evaluation of the tool execution in a simulated en-

This is the first step of the training phase. Here,
given a question, we prompt an LLM to generate
tools it thinks could be relevant for solving the
question (See Fig. 7 for Prompt Template). As

a question. These tools are then aligned with their gold tool (GT) counterparts. Finally, the aligned tool pairs are

evidence.source_content:
Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate retriever quality
using 4 standard IR (Information Retrieval) metrics.
These are (i) NDCG@K/N@K (Normalized Dis-
counted Cumulative Gain): evaluates the quality
of a ranked list by rewarding relevant items being
placed at the top of the list and penalizing them
being placed towards the bottom; (ii) P@K (Pre-

relevant to the search; (iii) R@K (Recall): The
fraction of relevant items that were retrieved, and

each measure, @K means the number of items that

The key
idea is that instead of relying on the LLM to generate verifi-
cation tests, we leverage the optimization solver to construct
simplified diagnostic queries about the original problem.
These simplified queries reduce complexity and probe spe-
cific properties while preserving the global semantic struc-

complexity along different problem dimensions represented
by constraints and decision variables, allowing us to probe
feasibility and optimality properties. Thus conceptually,
our approach inverts the conventional verification workflow:
instead of using the LLM to propose test scenarios that
are then checked by the solver, we leverage the solver’s

evidence.locator: P100:p0006:s0001; exact extracted span beginning 'The difficulty-bucket analysis at N=50 shows how the'
evidence.source_content:
The difficulty-bucket analysis at N=50 shows how the adaptation works. Because the candidate
sets are smaller, we use narrower buckets: ranked 1st, 2nd–3rd, 4th–10th, and 11+. On easy queries
(gold ranked 1st), all methods achieve 100% found, with the BoR agent stopping at K=1.58. On
medium queries (gold ranked 2nd–3rd), the BoR agent extends to K=3.72 and finds 79.3%, while
the F1 ablation at K=1.48 finds only 29.3% and Fixed K=1 finds 0%. On hard queries (gold ranked
4th–10th), the BoR agent increases to K=4.24 and finds 26.5%, while the ablation and Fixed K=1
find nothing.

ToolBench (3,251 tools, tool-level matching).  We use the official ToolBench data [27], matching
at the tool level rather than the API level.2 Because each tool exposes multiple APIs, we aggregate
API descriptions to the tool level and score them with MiniLM embeddings. We use 2,000 single-
tool queries (1,400 train / 600 test) and construct N=50 candidate sets from the gold tool plus hard
distractors, with 3 seeds. The BoR agent achieves 61.9 ± 0.6% at K=4.4 ± 0.4. The F1 ablation
achieves 47.6±1.3% at K=1.5±0.3, barely above FK=1 (45.3%). A common fixed-depth baseline,
FK=5, achieves 64.7%, while deeper baselines reach 77.3% (FK=20) at the cost of selectivity.

The difficulty-bucket analysis at N=50 shows the clearest separation between methods, with 3-seed
standard deviations indicating that the pattern is stable. On easy queries (gold ranked 1st, n=272),
the BoR agent uses K=2.5 ± 0.2 and achieves 100%. On medium queries (gold ranked 2nd–5th,
n=116), it increases to K=4.8 ± 0.5 and finds 74.4 ± 0.4%. FK=5 also finds 100% on medium
queries, but only by using the same depth for every query. On hard queries (gold ranked 6th–20th,
n=76), the BoR agent increases to K=5.7±0.5 and finds 16.7±4.3%, while FK=5, the F1 ablation,
and FK=1 all find 0%. On very hard queries (gold ranked 21+, n=136), the BoR agent increases
to K=6.9 ± 0.7 and finds 0.2%, while all alternatives find 0%. Overall, the F1 ablation finds only
47.6%.

The BoR agent adapts K from 2.5 to 6.9 based on query difficulty (Figure 1). By contrast, the F1
ablation stays near K≈1.5 across all buckets, while Fixed K=5 uses K=5 everywhere. On hard
queries, the BoR agent finds tools that every alternative misses entirely. FK=5 achieves higher ag-
gregate coverage (64.7% vs 61.9%). This reflects its uniform depth: it catches all easy and medium
queries (where gold is ranked 1–5) but finds nothing on hard and very hard queries (where gold is
ranked 6+). The BoR agent trades some medium-query coverage for recovery on hard queries.
evidence.codex_note: Fixed depth zeroes hard-query coverage (FK=5/F1/FK=1 all 0% on gold-rank 6-20) while winning aggregate coverage - aggregate metrics mask distributional failure.

evidence.locator: P101:p0002:s0001; exact extracted span beginning 'Our search objective is formally deﬁned through neighbor'
evidence.source_content:
Our search objective is formally deﬁned through
neighbor queries (Section 3.1), which are gener-
ated by modifying one aspect of the gold query.
For example, prediction 1 in Figure 1 is a neigh-
bor query of the gold, since they diﬀer only by a
“WHERE” clause. These neighbor queries are usu-
ally semantically diﬀerent from the gold, and if a
test suite can distinguish them from the gold, it is
likely to distinguish other wrong queries as well.
The latter holds because distinguishing all neigh-
bors from the gold requires executions on these
databases to exercise every modiﬁed part of the
gold query, hence reﬂecting comprehensive code
coverage and high test quality (Miller and Maloney,
1963; Ammann and Oﬀutt). Hence, we formalize
our objective as ﬁnding a small test suite that can
distinguish all the neighbors (Section 3.2).
evidence.codex_note: Distillation operator: single-modification neighbor queries define a coverage criterion; a test suite distinguishing all neighbors exercises every modified part of the gold query.
